To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) food prices are volatile, but the extent of volatility varies across countries and commodities, (ii) price instability has adverse effects on food consumption, poverty, and food security, (iii) food market reforms have been successful in many countries, but have not been successful in others, (iv) policy reforms should be sequenced to promote efficiency and stability in food markets, and (v) policy responses to price instability should be designed to protect the interests of consumers and the poor.
food market reforms in many countries have been accompanied by significant price instability and that this instability has imposed significant economic and social costs on the poor.

(i) price instability is an important issue for the food security of the poor, and (ii) the poor are hurt more by price instability than the non-poor, and the poor suffer the most when price instability is high.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of policies and programs that promote food security, poverty reduction, and sustainable development in the midst of liberalizing markets.
the design of policy reform and the design of policy responses to food market instability.
the following question: how can food markets be reformed to promote efficient and stable development and protect the poor in a liberalizing environment?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
food prices are generally stable in most of the developing world, but that price instability can be a serious problem in some countries.
there is no simple answer to the question of what policies are needed to promote stable and efficient food markets.
there is no one-size-fits-all approach to managing price risks and food market reforms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) food market reforms have generally led to improved food market efficiency and stability; (ii) there are significant country differences in the extent of market reforms, the sources of price instability, and the costs of food price instability; (ii) food market reforms are likely to be more difficult to sustain in the face of price shocks; (iii) there are no simple policy solutions to food price instability; and (iv) there is a need to strengthen the institutional capacity of policy makers to deal
the poor are hurt most by price instability, and that the costs of instability are likely to rise as markets liberalize, unless policy makers take steps to address them.

food price instability is a major problem for the world’s poor, but it can be reduced through a range of policy reforms that promote market development, including the removal of trade barriers and the adoption of appropriate safety net programs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single policy response to the problem of food price instability.
food price instability has been a persistent feature of the global food system, with the magnitude and sources of instability varying by country and region.
food market liberalization is a necessary condition for reducing food price instability, but not sufficient.
